, such that

\displaystyle|{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\rangle_{BB^{\prime}C}=\sum_{k=1}^{d_{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}|k\rangle_{BB^{\prime}}\otimes|k\rangle_{C}.

(103)

The teleportation condition can be rewritten as follows, tracing out over the ancilla: for all density matrix
\rho_{A}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{A})
,

\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}_{BB^{\prime}}[{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{AB}\rho_{A}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{BB^{\prime}C}]=p_{\textsc{tp}}\rho_{C}.

(104)

Now, we define the orthogonal projector

\displaystyle\Pi_{BB^{\prime}}:=\sum_{k=1}^{d_{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}}|k\rangle\langle k|_{BB^{\prime}}.

(105)

This projector is such that
\Pi_{BB^{\prime}}|{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\rangle_{BB^{\prime}C}=|{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\rangle_{BB^{\prime}C}
.
We then define

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{ABB^{\prime}}:=(\mathbbm{1}_{A}\otimes\Pi_{BB^{\prime}})({\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{AB}\otimes\mathbbm{1}_{B^{\prime}})(\mathbbm{1}_{A}\otimes\Pi_{BB^{\prime}}),

(106)

which can be checked to be a valid POVM element.
Using the “partial cyclicity” of the partial trace,
equation

104
is equivalent to

\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}_{BB^{\prime}}[{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{ABB^{\prime}}\rho_{A}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{BB^{\prime}C}]=p_{\textsc{tp}}\rho_{C}.

(107)

We let
\{|k\rangle_{A}\}_{k=1}^{d_{A}}
be the orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{H}_{A}
that corresponds to the orthonormal basis
\{|k\rangle_{C}\}_{k}
of
\mathcal{H}_{C}
through the identity that the teleportation protocol assumes, namely,
\mathcal{H}_{A}=\mathcal{H}_{C}
.
Since the teleportation probability
p_{\textsc{tp}}
does not depend on
\rho
, we can use the linearity of
equation

107
, together with the fact that the linear span of density matrices consists of all (possibly non-Hermitian) linear operators on the Hilbert space, to substitute
|i\rangle\langle j|_{A}
instead of
\rho_{A}
.
Then, we have for all
i,j\in\{1,\dots,d_{A}\}
,

\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}_{BB^{\prime}}[{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{ABB^{\prime}}|i\rangle\langle j|_{A}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{BB^{\prime}C}]=p_{\textsc{tp}}|i\rangle\langle j|_{C}.

(108)

Introducing the Schmidt decomposition of
equation

103
, we obtain

\displaystyle\sum_{k,l=1}^{d_{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{l}\langle j|_{A}\langle l|_{BB^{\prime}}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{ABB^{\prime}}|i\rangle_{A}|k\rangle_{BB^{\prime}}|k\rangle\langle l|_{C}=p_{\textsc{tp}}|i\rangle\langle j|_{C}.

(109)

This directly implies that
d_{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}=d_{A}
, which in turn implies that
d_{B}d_{B^{\prime}}\geq d_{A}
.
Furthemore, we can solve
equation

109
for
{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{ABB^{\prime}}
: for all
i,j\in\{1,\dots,d_{A}\}
, for all
l,k\in\{1,\dots,d_{A}\}
,

\displaystyle\langle j|_{A}\langle l|_{BB^{\prime}}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{ABB^{\prime}}|i\rangle_{A}|k\rangle_{BB^{\prime}}=\frac{p_{\textsc{tp}}}{{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{l}}\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}.

(110)

This yields

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{ABB^{\prime}}=\Pi_{BB^{\prime}}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{ABB^{\prime}}\Pi_{BB^{\prime}}=p_{\textsc{tp}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{d_{A}}\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{l}}|k\rangle\langle l|_{A}\otimes|k\rangle\langle l|_{BB^{\prime}}=:|{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}\rangle\langle{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}|_{ABB^{\prime}},

(111)

where we defined the following sub-normalized state:

\displaystyle|{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}\rangle_{ABB^{\prime}}=\sqrt{p_{\textsc{tp}}}\sum_{k=1}^{d_{A}}\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}}|k\rangle_{A}|k\rangle_{BB^{\prime}}.

(112)

Note that for
{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{ABB^{\prime}}
to be a valid POVM element, we need
{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{ABB^{\prime}}\leq\mathbbm{1}_{ABB^{\prime}}
, which implies that the norm of the above state must be at most one, implying the inequality of
equation

97
.
∎

We can now prove that the optimal teleportation probability is given by
1/d_{A}^{2}
, which is achieved by the Bell state preparation and measurement of
definition

5
.

Lemma 27

(Maximal teleportation probability)
.

Given
\mathcal{H}_{A}=\mathcal{H}_{C}
, the maximal teleportation probability
p_{\textsc{tp}}
that can be achieved within
definition

4
is
1/d_{A}^{2}
.

Proof.

First, we have seen that the teleportation probability
p_{\textsc{tp}}=1/d_{A}^{2}
is always achievable by the Bell state implementation of
definition

5
.
Indeed, we can put this implementation in the form of
lemma

26
: we have
{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{A}}}
, and the pure state
|E\rangle_{BB^{\prime}C}=|\Phi^{+}\rangle_{BB^{\prime}C}
defining the POVM element of the implementation can be written as

\displaystyle|E\rangle_{BB^{\prime}C}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{d_{A}^{2}}}\sum_{k=1}^{d_{A}}\sqrt{d_{A}}|k\rangle_{BB^{\prime}}\otimes|k\rangle_{C},

(113)

thus showing that for this protocol,
p_{\textsc{tp}}=1/d_{A}^{2}
.

We now wish to show that any teleportation probability is upper-bounded by
1/d_{A}^{2}
.
For a vector
\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}=({\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k})_{k}
, we denote with
\lVert\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\lVert^{2}=\sum_{k}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}^{2}
the Euclidean norm squared.
First, we argue that the maximal teleportation probability is given by

\displaystyle\max\Big\{p_{\textsc{tp}}\,\Big|\,\exists\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{A}}:\ {\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}\neq 0,\lVert\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\lVert^{2}=1\textup{ and }\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{d_{A}}\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{p_{\textsc{tp}}}\Big\}

(114)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\max\Big\{p_{\textsc{tp}}\,\Big|\,\exists\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{A}}:\ {\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}\neq 0,\lVert\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\lVert^{2}=1\textup{ and }\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{d_{A}}\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}^{2}}=\frac{1}{p_{\textsc{tp}}}\Big\}

(115)

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\max\Big\{p_{\textsc{tp}}\,\Big|\,\exists\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi},\vec{\psi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{A}}:\ \lVert\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\lVert^{2}=1\textup{ and }\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\cdot\vec{\psi}=d_{A}\textup{ and }\lVert\vec{\psi}\lVert^{2}=\textstyle\frac{1}{p_{\textsc{tp}}}\Big\},

(116)

where the last inequality follows from seeing that any
p_{\textsc{tp}}
achievable for some
\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}
in
equation

115
can be achieved by using the same
\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}
in
equation

116
together with setting
\psi_{k}=1/{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}
.
To maximize
p_{\textsc{tp}}
, we need to minimize the norm of
\vec{\psi}
.
However, subject to the constraints
\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\cdot\vec{\psi}=d_{A}
and
\lVert\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\lVert=1
, this means that we need to pick
\vec{\psi}=d_{A}\vec{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}
, so that
\lVert\vec{\psi}\lVert^{2}=d_{A}^{2}
, and the maximum teleportation probability is indeed
1/d_{A}^{2}
.
∎

We now prove the following lemma, which will allow us to prove that the probabilities associated to cyclic causal models according to our proposed probability rule do not depend on the choice of post-selected teleportation implementation.

Lemma 28

(Cyclic composition is independent of post-selected teleportation implementation)
.

It holds that for all post-selected teleportation implementation
({\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{AB},{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{BC})
with associated teleportation probability
p_{\textsc{tp}}
(see
definition

4
),

\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}_{AB}[{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{AB}\mathcal{M}_{A|C}({\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{BC})]=p_{\textsc{tp}}\,\mathrm{cycle}(\mathcal{M}_{A|C}),

(117)

where
\mathrm{cycle}(\mathcal{M}_{A|C})
is defined in
definition

13
.

Proof.

Consider an arbitrary post-selected teleportation implementation
({\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{AB},{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{BC})
with associated teleportation probability
p_{\textsc{tp}}
, and let
\mathcal{H}_{B^{\prime}}
,
\{|k\rangle_{A}\}_{k=1}^{d}
,
\{|k\rangle_{BB^{\prime}}\}_{k=1}^{d}
,
|{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\rangle_{BB^{\prime}C}
and
|{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}\rangle_{ABB^{\prime}}
be as in
lemma

26
.
We then have

\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}_{AB}[{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}_{AB}\mathcal{M}_{A|C}({\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{BC})]

\displaystyle=\mathrm{Tr}_{ABB^{\prime}}[|{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}\rangle\langle{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}|_{ABB^{\prime}}\mathcal{M}_{A|C}(|{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}\rangle\langle{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}|_{BB^{\prime}C})]

\displaystyle=\sum_{k,l,m,n=1}^{d}\mathrm{Tr}_{ABB^{\prime}}\left[\frac{p_{\textsc{tp}}}{{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{m}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{n}}|m\rangle\langle n|_{A}\otimes|m\rangle\langle n|_{BB^{\prime}}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{k}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}_{l}|k\rangle\langle l|_{BB^{\prime}}\otimes\mathcal{M}_{A|C}(|k\rangle\langle l|_{C})\right]

\displaystyle=p_{\textsc{tp}}\,\mathrm{cycle}(\mathcal{M}_{A|C}).\qed

(118)

Appendix B
Links to other quantum causality frameworks

B.1
Barrett Lorenz Oreshkov cyclic causal models

In this section, we outline relationships and distinctions between our framework and the cyclic quantum causal modelling formalism of Barrett, Lorenz and Oreshkov (BLO)
[
BLO21
]
. We show that whenever the output space of each party
A_{i}
factorises into tensor factors, one for each child of the vertex
A_{i}
, then such causal models in the BLO framework can be recovered faithfully within our framework. This tensor factor restriction of the BLO framework can be seen as a natural cyclic generalization of the acyclic causal modelling framework of Costa and Shrapnel
[
CS16
]
, thus in particular, the latter is also recovered in our framework. We then discuss the prospects for faithfully mapping the more general case (without the tensor factor restriction)
into our framework and its links to the causal decomposition problem.

B.1.1
Review of the BLO formalism

We begin by outlining how cyclic causal models are defined in the BLO formalism, the main ingredients are the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism
[
Cho75
,
Jam72
]
and the concept of process operators.

Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism.

With every linear completely positive (CP) map,
\mathcal{E}_{A\mapsto B}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{A})\mapsto\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{B})
, we can associate a corresponding Choi-Jamiolkowski (CJ) operator,

\rho_{B|A}=\sum_{i,j}\mathcal{E}_{A\mapsto B}\left(|i\rangle\langle j|_{A}\right)\otimes|i\rangle\langle j|_{A^{*}}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{B})\otimes\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{A}^{*}),

(119)

where
\{|i\rangle_{A}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{H}_{A}
and
\{|i\rangle_{A^{*}}\}
is the corresponding dual basis (an orthonormal basis of the dual space
\mathcal{H}_{A}^{*}
). When the map is completely positive and trace preserving (CPTP), we have
\mathrm{Tr}_{B}(\rho_{B|A})=\mathbbm{1}_{A^{*}}
. The inverse isomorphism is given as follows and allows us to compute the action of the channel
\mathcal{E}_{A\mapsto B}
on an input state
\rho_{A}
:
\mathcal{E}_{A\mapsto B}(\rho_{A})=\mathrm{Tr}[\tau^{\textup{id}}_{AA^{*}}\rho_{B|A}\rho_{A}]
, where
\tau^{\textup{id}}_{AA^{*}}=\sum_{i,j}|i\rangle\langle j|_{A}\otimes|i\rangle\langle j|_{A^{*}}
is known as the linking operator. This equation has a striking similarity to classical conditional probabilities (which describe the action of classical channels)
\mathcal{P}(Y)=\sum_{X}\mathcal{P}(Y|X)\mathcal{P}(X)

[
LS13
]
, where
\mathcal{P}
denotes an arbitrary probability distribution over two random variables
X
and
Y
.

There are multiple versions of the CJ isomorphism (see for instance
[
FC24
]
), the above version is chosen in the BLO formalism as it is basis independent and yields a positive CJ operator. In particular, the more commonly used version is

\rho^{(1)}_{B|A}=\sum_{i,j}\mathcal{E}_{A\mapsto B}(|i\rangle\langle j|_{A})\otimes|i\rangle\langle j|_{A}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{B})\otimes\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{A}),

(120)

which is positive but basis dependent, and another version is given by

\rho_{B|A}^{(2)}:=\sum_{i,j}\mathcal{E}_{A\mapsto B}(|i\rangle\langle j|_{A})\otimes|j\rangle\langle i|_{A}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{B})\otimes\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{A}),

(121)

which is basis-independent but not necessarily positive. The inverse isomorphisms in these cases are given as
\mathcal{E}_{A\mapsto B}(\rho_{A})=\mathrm{Tr}[\rho^{(1)}_{B|A}(\mathbbm{1}_{B}\otimes\rho_{A}^{T})]=\mathrm{Tr}[\rho^{(2)}_{B|A}(\mathbbm{1}_{B}\otimes\rho_{A})]
.

Process operators and probabilities.

The next ingredient is the concept of process operators, which was previously used in the process matrix
[
OCB12
]

and higher-order quantum process
[
CDPV13
]
frameworks. The idea is to consider multiple laboratories
A_{1},...,A_{N}
, each
A_{i}
being associated with a pair of in and output spaces
A_{i}^{\textup{in}}:=\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{in}}}\right)
,
A_{i}^{\textup{out}}:=\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{out}}}\right)
. An agent may perform a local quantum operation within each such lab, which corresponds to a quantum instrument, i.e., a set of CP maps
\{\mathcal{M}_{x_{i}}:A_{i}^{\textup{in}}\mapsto A_{i}^{\textup{out}}\}_{x_{i}}
such that
\mathcal{M}:=\sum_{x_{i}}\mathcal{M}_{x_{i}}
is CPTP. Generally, the local operations can be parametrised by a classical setting choice
a_{i}
and we have a corresponding quantum instrument
\{\mathcal{M}_{x_{i}|a_{i}}\}_{x_{i}}
. The process operator
\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}\in\mathcal{L}\left(\bigotimes_{i}\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{in}}}\bigotimes_{i}\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{out}}}^{*}\right)
describes the environment of these labs, and encodes information on how they are connected, for instance whether or not there is a channel connecting the output
A_{1}^{\textup{out}}
of lab
A_{1}
to the input
A_{2}^{\textup{in}}
of the next lab
A_{2}
.
The outcome probabilities can be computed as follows

\textup{Pr}_{\textup{BLO}}(x_{1},...,x_{N}|a_{1},...,a_{N})=\mathrm{Tr}\left[\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}\Big(\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\rho_{A^{\textup{out}}_{i}|A^{\textup{in}}_{i}}^{x_{i}|a_{i}}\Big)^{T}\right],

(122)

where
\rho_{A^{\textup{out}}_{i}|A^{\textup{in}}_{i}}^{x_{i}|a_{i}}
denotes the CJ operator of the local operation
\mathcal{M}_{x_{i}|a_{i}}
.

The conditions for
\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}
being a valid process operator
17
17

17

These include that
\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}>0
and
\mathrm{Tr}\Big[\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}\Big(\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\rho_{A^{\textup{out}}_{i}|A^{\textup{in}}_{i}}\Big)^{T}\Big]=1
when
\rho_{A^{\textup{out}}_{i}|A^{\textup{in}}_{i}}
are CJ operators of CPTP maps.
ensure that the distribution defined above is a valid, normalised probability distribution. See
[
ABC+15
]
and
[
OG16
]
for further details on necessary and sufficient constraints on valid process operators. In the above, all output spaces appearing in the CJ operators
\rho_{A^{\textup{out}}_{i}|A^{\textup{in}}_{i}}
and the process operator
\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}
are the dual spaces
\mathcal{H}^{*}_{A_{i}^{\textup{out}}}
.

We could alternatively use the CJ operators according to the variant
\rho^{(1)}_{A^{\textup{out}}_{i}|A^{\textup{in}}_{i}}
of the CJ isomorphism where the dual spaces do not feature, and define the process operator on the joint in and output spaces of all parties. One can show that the probability expression
equation

122
will be identical.
However, in the latter case, one must be careful to express all operators and take the transpose in the same basis. We are now ready to review the definition of causal models in this framework.

Definition 29

(BLO-QCM
[
BLO21
]
)
.

A BLO-QCM is given by

1.

A causal structure which corresponds to a directed graph
G
with vertices
A_{1},...,A_{N}

2.

For each
A_{i}
, a quantum channel (in CJ representation)

\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}\in\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{in}}}\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{A_{k}\in\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}\mathcal{H}^{*}_{A_{k}^{\textup{out}}}\right)\right)

where
\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})
denotes the set of all parents of
A_{i}
in
G
, such that

[\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})},\sigma_{A_{j}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{j})}]=0

for all
i,j
and
\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}
is a valid process operator.

Note that the original papers
[
BLO20
,
BLO21
]
use
\rho_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}
rather than
\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}
for the channels mentioned in the above definition. We employ the latter notation in order to make it clear that these are internal channels of the process operator as opposed to the channels
\rho_{A_{i}^{\textup{out}}|A_{i}^{\textup{in}}}
corresponding to the external operations performed by the parties.

The BLO framework focuses process operators
\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}
which correspond to the CJ operator of a unitary channel from the outputs of all parties to their inputs. Generally, given a channel
\mathcal{E}
, the dependence of an output
O
of a channel
\mathcal{E}
on an input
I
is checked by whether a choice
\mathcal{M}_{I}
of local operation on
I
can lead to distinguishable states on
O
, i.e., we have signalling from
I
to
O
through
\mathcal{E}
when
\mathrm{Tr}_{\backslash O}\circ\mathcal{E}\circ\mathcal{M}_{I}\neq\mathrm{Tr}_{\backslash O}\circ\mathcal{E}
, where
\backslash O
denotes all outputs of
\mathcal{E}
except
O
(see
[
OVB23
]
for equivalent definitions).
If the channel is unitary, the signalling relations between in and outputs form a directed acyclic graph where the in and output systems are the vertices
[
BLO20
]
. This is not the case for general CPTP maps, where we can have non-trivial signalling relations between subsets of systems without signalling between individual systems, e.g., an input
I
of a (non-unitary) CPTP map
\mathcal{E}
can signal to outputs
O_{1}
and
O_{2}
jointly but not individually.

Therefore, for unitary channels one can construct the edges of the graph through signalling relations, i.e., the parents of every output system
S
,
\mathrm{Pa}(S)
, correspond to inputs that signal to
S
through the unitary channel.
If we apply such construction to the unitary channel of the process operator, the factorisation

\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}

can be derived as a theorem (Theorem 4.3 of
[
BLO20
]
).
The factors are marginals of the full channel and commute with each other as required by
definition

29
. This motivates using such signalling relations to define causal relations in the case of unitary channels as processes — which is the case in the BLO framework. For further details on causality in unitary channels, we refer the reader to
[
ABH+17
,
BLO20
,
BLO21
]
. For details on the inequivalence between causation and signalling in non-unitary channels, we refer the reader to the above and to
[
VR24a
]
.

B.1.2
Tensor restriction of the BLO formalism and mapping to our framework

At this point, we can observe an important distinction between causal models in ours and the BLO formalism. Consider a simple common cause graph where we have vertices
A
,
B
and
C
and directed edges
(A,B)
and
(A,C)
. In our formalism, any causal model on this graph will have a channel
\mathcal{E}^{A}
which has two outgoing wires, one for each outgoing edge and no incoming wires as
A
is exogenous (i.e., a bipartite state preparation), while
B
and
C
will be associated with channels
\mathcal{E}^{B}
and
\mathcal{E}^{C}
acting on the sub-systems of the bipartite state sent along the respective edges, i.e.,

(123)

In the BLO formalism, a common cause structure emanating from
A
does not generally imply a channel at
A
with multiple outgoing wires (each associated with a separate system).
More specifically, considering the three vertices as three labs and using trivial in/output spaces for exogenous or childless vertices, we notice that the BLO framework associates a single global channel from the output space
A^{\textup{out}}
of
A
to the inputs
B^{\textup{in}}
and
C^{\textup{in}}
whose CJ operator is
\sigma_{BC|A}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{B^{\textup{in}}}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{C^{\textup{in}}}\otimes\mathcal{H}^{*}_{A^{\textup{out}}})
(this would in fact be the process operator, if we ignore the trivial spaces), with commuting marginals
[\sigma_{B|A},\sigma_{C|A}]=0
(keeping factors of identity implicit),
\sigma_{B|A}=\mathrm{Tr}_{C}(\sigma_{BC|A})
and
\sigma_{C|A}=\mathrm{Tr}_{B}(\sigma_{BC|A})
. Generally,
A
could be a qubit and need not factorise into independent tensor factors corresponding to two wires.

In the BLO formalism, a vertex
A
corresponds to (pairs of) systems,
\mathcal{H}_{A^{\textup{in}}}
and
\mathcal{H}_{A^{\textup{out}}}
and the edge structure specifies the channels
\sigma_{A|\mathrm{Pa}(A)}
that connect the in/output systems between vertices. By contrast, in our formalism vertices
v
are associated with channels
\mathcal{E}^{v}
while edges
e
are associated with systems
\mathcal{H}_{e}
. How should we compare and map between the frameworks in a faithful manner that preserves the relevant information?

Faithful mappings and tensor-restriction of BLO models.

We now show that if we require a tensor factorisation of output spaces in the BLO framework in terms of the structure of outgoing edges, then there is a faithful mapping into out framework for every choice of local operations. More formally, we first define these concepts, starting with defining when a mapping between two quantum causality formalisms can be considered faithful. As different frameworks formalize causal models in distinct ways, we will use a more general terminology that captures the essential features of such models: a
quantum causal description
consists of a directed graph together with an assignment of causal mechanisms (quantum channels) to that graph, and a rule for computing observed correlations arising from those mechanisms.

Definition 30

(Faithful mapping between quantum causal descriptions)
.

We say that a mapping from one quantum causal description to another is faithful if

(a)

all the vertices and associated causal mechanisms of the former are preserved in the image of the mapping,

(b)

if there is no directed path from
A_{i}
to
A_{j}
in the former, then there will be no directed path from
A_{i}
to
A_{j}
in the latter,

(c)

the probability rules associated with both descriptions lead to the same observed correlations.

This usage of the term faithful is also consistent with its formal usage in causal modelling and inference parlance. There, a causal model is said to be faithful if whenever there is connectivity in the graph, there is a corresponding conditional dependence in the causal model. If we mapped a BLO-QCM to our framework in a way that reproduces the operational predictions but there are additional directed paths in the causal graph of the image than the original model specifies, then the final causal model will generally not be faithful to the graph as it will contain additional observable independences not reflected in the connectivity (see
section

B.2
for further details). Note that any reasonable graph-separation notion would regard
A_{i}
and
A_{j}
as connected when there is a directed path from one to the other, i.e., when one is a cause of the other (
d
,
\sigma
and
p
separation satisfy this).

Next, we define the tensor-restriction of BLO quantum causal models as follows.

Definition 31

(BLO-QCM
⊗
)
.

We define a tensor product restricted BLO-QCM, denoted BLO-QCM
⊗
as being specified by the following.

1.

A causal structure which corresponds to directed graph
G
with vertices
A_{1},...,A_{N}
.

2.

For each
A_{i}
, a tensor factorisation of its output space as
\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{out}}}=\bigotimes_{A_{k}\in\mathrm{Ch}(A_{i})}\mathcal{H}_{A_{ik}^{\textup{out}}}
where
\mathrm{Ch}(A_{i})
denotes the set of all children of
A_{i}
in
G
and
\mathcal{H}_{A_{ik}^{\textup{out}}}
are arbitrary finite dimensional Hilbert spaces.

3.

For each
A_{i}
, a quantum channel

\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}\in\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{in}}}\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{A_{k}\in\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}\mathcal{H}^{*}_{A_{ki}^{\textup{out}}}\right)\right)

such that
\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}
is a valid process operator.

Since each channel
\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}
acts on a distinct Hilbert space (distinct tensor factors of the parental Hilbert space), the commutation condition
[\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})},\sigma_{A_{j}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{j})}]=0
is satisfied for all
i,j
.
Hence, every BLO-QCM
⊗
is indeed an instance of a general BLO-QCM.

Faithfully mapping a tensor restricted BLO-QCM to our formalism.

We now show that
any BLO-QCM
⊗
(
definition

31
) can be faithfully mapped (
definition

30
) into our framework. Given a BLO-QCM
⊗
together with a choice of quantum instrument
\mathcal{M}_{a_{i}}:=\{\mathcal{M}_{x_{i}|a_{i}}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{in}}})\mapsto\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{out}}})\}_{x_{i}}
, one for each agent
A_{i}
, we can obtain a causal model in our formalism (
definition

2
) through the mapping we describe below.
Therefore, each BLO-QCM
⊗
maps to a family of QCMs in our framework, with each element in the family corresponding to a fixed choice of instruments for the
N
parties, labelled by the settings {
a_{i}\}_{i}
. A previous causal modelling framework by Costa and Shrapnel
[
CS16
]
can be seen as a further restriction of BLO-QCM
⊗
above to the case of directed acyclic graphs
G
. Hence, the mapping we give here shows that the Costa and Shrapnel formalism can also be faithfully recovered within ours.

•

Causal graph
If
G
is the graph associated with the given BLO-QCM
⊗
, by construction it has
N
vertices
\{A_{1},...,A_{N}\}
. Without loss of generality, let
\{A_{1},...,A_{k}\}
denote the vertices associated with a trivial (1-dimensional) input Hilbert space.

Define a new causal graph
G^{\prime}
constructed from
G
as follows with
2N+k
vertices:
\{A_{1},...,A_{N}\}\cup\{\sigma_{1},...,\sigma_{k}\}\cup\{X_{1},...,X_{N}\}
, where
\{X_{1},...,X_{N}\}
are observed while the rest are unobserved vertices. Whenever
(A_{i},A_{j})
is a directed edge in
G
,
A_{j}
cannot have a trivial input space, and we include a corresponding directed edge
(A_{i},\sigma_{j})
in
G^{\prime}
. Further, include directed edges
(\sigma_{j},A_{j})
for every
j\not\in\{1,...,k\}
and
(A_{j},X_{j})
for all
j\in\{1,...,N\}
in
G^{\prime}
. This construction ensures that
absence of directed paths in
G
implies the same in
G^{\prime}
as required by
definition

30
.

•

State spaces
We now associate a state space to each edge on the causal graph
G^{\prime}
as required by
definition

2
. Consider the edges
(A_{i},\sigma_{j})
of
G^{\prime}
, which correspond to edges
(A_{i},A_{j})
of
G
. Since each BLO-QCM
⊗
assigns a tensor factor
\mathcal{H}_{A_{ij}^{\textup{out}}}
of
A_{i}
’s output space
\mathcal{H}_{A^{\textup{out}}_{i}}
to every child
A_{j}
of
A_{i}
, we can assign this space to the edge
(A_{i},\sigma_{j})
of
G^{\prime}
. The edges
(\sigma_{j},A_{j})
are incoming to the lab
A_{j}
and will be associated with the input space
\mathcal{H}_{A_{j}^{\textup{in}}}
. The edges
(A_{j},X_{j})
model the influence of each party’s action on their classical outcome, and will be associated a Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{X}_{j})
which encodes the outcome set of the
j
-th party
\mathcal{X}_{j}:=\{x_{j}\}_{x_{j}}
in a preferred basis.

•

Quantum channels
In this mapping, we will ignore the dual spaces of the BLO framework. This is not an issue, as discussed earlier, as long as we are consistent about taking transposes in the same basis in which the CJ operators are expressed. Each of the
\sigma_{i}
vertices is assigned the quantum channel
\hat{\sigma}_{i}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{in}}})\mapsto\mathcal{L}(\bigotimes_{A_{k}\in\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}\mathcal{H}_{A_{ki}^{\textup{out}}})
whose CJ operator is the operator
\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}
of the BLO framework
18
18

18

According to the basis-dependent CJ representation without the dual spaces (
equation

120
). We referred to this with a superscript 1 before but drop this to avoid clutter, since the meaning is clear from context.
. Each of the
A_{i}
vertices is assigned the corresponding local quantum instrument,
\mathcal{M}_{a_{i}}
with a slight modification to make explicit the outcome as a separate system. The modified instrument is associated with a CPTP map
\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{a_{i}}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{in}}})\mapsto\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{out}}}\otimes\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{X}_{i}))
defined as follows (where each term in the sum below is a CP map
\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{x_{i}|a_{i}}
, the set of which defines the instrument)

\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{a_{i}}(\rho_{A^{\textup{in}}_{i}}):=\sum_{x_{i}}\mathcal{M}_{x_{i}|a_{i}}(\rho_{A_{i}^{\textup{in}}})\otimes|x_{i}\rangle\langle x_{i}|.

(124)

Finally, the
X_{i}
vertices are associated with a set of maps
\{\mathcal{E}_{x_{i}}\}_{x_{i}}
specified by a POVM which has elements
E_{x_{i}}:=|x_{i}\rangle\langle x_{i}|
, according to
equation

19
(we have used
\mathcal{E}
for this map as opposed to
\mathcal{M}
of the defining equation, in order to distinguish this from the maps assigned to the labs). Note that the in and output spaces of all channels in this step match with the state spaces assigned to the in/outgoing edges in the previous step.

•

Probabilities
The above fully specifies a causal model according to
definition

2
, for every BLO-QCM
⊗
and choice
\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}
of local instruments. We can now show that the probabilities
\textup{Pr}_{\textup{BLO}}(x_{1},...,x_{N}|a_{1},...,a_{N})
as computed in the BLO formalism (
equation

122
) and using the probability rule of our formalism (
section

4.3
) would be the same.

⊗
.

and

(126)

Notice that the absence of directed paths from
D
to
C
in
G
is also reflected in
G^{\prime}
, in accordance with
definition

30
.
We now explain why the observed probabilities are the same under this mapping.

Consider a causal model on the causal graph
G^{\prime}
obtained from a BLO-QCM
⊗
through the mapping that we have described above. We can construct an acyclic causal graph
\overline{G^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{G}_{\textsc{tp}}(G^{\prime})
by replacing each of the edges
(A_{i},\sigma_{j})
of
G^{\prime}
(which arise from the edges
(A_{i},A_{j})
of the BLO-QCM
⊗
) with a post-selected teleportation protocol. Suppose there are
k
edges of the type

A_{i}
\sigma_{j}

. We then have the pre and post-selection vertices
\{R_{1},\dots,R_{k}\}=V_{\textup{pre}}
and
\{T_{1},\dots,T_{k}\}=V_{\textup{post}}
, and each such edge is replaced with the following protocol for a pair
(R_{l},T_{l})
:

A_{i}
\sigma_{j}
R_{l}
T_{l}
(R_{l},T_{l})
e_{l}
e_{l}^{\prime}

Then we can define a family of causal models on the acyclic causal graph
\overline{G^{\prime}}
based on any given causal model on the original graph
G^{\prime}
: for all the original edges and vertices, all the causal mechanisms are the same and we assign a post-selection teleportation protocol specified by pre and post-selection mechanisms
({\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}^{l},{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}^{l})
to each pair of pre and post-selection vertices
(R_{l},T_{l})
and associated edges. This is a family since we have a choice over the pre and post-selection mechanisms
({\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}^{l},{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}^{l})
that result in a post-selected teleportation protocol (
definition

4
).
Using the acyclic probability rule, the required probability
\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}(x_{1},...,x_{N}|a_{1},..,a_{N})_{G^{\prime}}
of the original causal model on
G^{\prime}
is then given as follows.

\begin{split}\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}(x_{1},...,x_{N}|&a_{1},..,a_{N})_{G^{\prime}}=\\
&\frac{\bigotimes_{l=1}^{k}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}^{l}\bigcomp_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{E}_{x_{i}}\bigcomp_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{x_{i}|a_{i}}\bigcomp_{i=1}^{N}\hat{\sigma}_{i}(\bigotimes_{l=1}^{k}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}^{l})}{\sum_{y_{1},...,y_{N}}\bigotimes_{l=1}^{k}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}^{l}\bigcomp_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{E}_{y_{i}}\bigcomp_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{y_{i}|a_{i}}\bigcomp_{i=1}^{N}\hat{\sigma}_{i}(\bigotimes_{l=1}^{k}{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}^{l})}.\end{split}

(127)

In the above, the composition rule is dictated by the acyclic graph
\overline{G^{\prime}}
(
definition

3
) and some factors of identity have been suppressed for brevity. The fraction form of the above expression is due to the usual conditional probability rule (Bayes rule). The numerator is the joint probability of obtaining the outcomes
x_{i}
and the post-selections given by
{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}^{l}
succeeding, while the denominator is just the probability of the latter. The fraction thus gives us the probability of the outcomes conditioned on post-selection success, which is what yields the required probabilities of the cyclic model (
definition

12
).

In
proposition

14
, it is shown that this expression can be equivalently written in terms of self-cycle composition, which is independent of the choice of
{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}E}^{l}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.7891,0.0781,0.1133}\varphi}^{l}
. For this, define

and apply a similar channel decomposition for the common cause edges from

, the total unitary channel from

given by the BLO formalism, would decompose into sub-channels such that the absence of a directed edge/path from
D
to

in the graph is reflected in the absence of a directed path of wires in the decomposition. This would allow a faithful mapping into our framework. It is shown in

[
ABH+17
]
that such direct-sum decompositions of the Choi states exist also when
A
is a common cause of any number
n
of vertices, allowing this case also to be mapped faithfully to our framework by considering the corresponding decomposition at the level of the channels. Thus, it is in principle possible to construct faithful mappings to our framework for BLO causal models that do not belong to BLO-QCM
⊗
.

An interesting open question is whether such faithful decompositions (where the connectivity of the wires in the circuit decomposition matches the connectivity of the causal graph) exist for all valid causal models in the BLO formalism. This question of causal decomposition is an important one in the quantum causal modelling literature, and the question can be refined by specifying the subset of channels with respect to which one seeks a decomposition of the original channel. In particular, causal decompositions of unitary channels in terms of smaller unitary channels has been studied and has led to interesting possibility and potential impossibility results in a range of directed acyclic graphs (defined relative to the signalling structure of the original unitary, as in the BLO framework)
[
LB21
]
. For there to exist a faithful mapping of every BLO causal model to our formalism, it is sufficient if the overall unitary channel defined in the BLO formalism admits a faithful causal decomposition in terms of general (not necessarily restricted to unitary) quantum channels. This remains an open problem even in acyclic causal models, and we are not aware of any counter-examples to show that this is not possible.

We leave a further investigation of this for future work. We note that unfaithful mappings into our formalism still exist for all process matrices and therefore for BLO-QCMs (based on unitary process matrices), and discuss this in the next subsection.

Process matrix protocols within our framework.

In usual quantum protocols, operations occur in a well-defined and acyclic order. Frameworks for modelling so-called indefinite causal order processes have been proposed (e.g.,
[
Har05
,
Har09
,
OCB12
,
CDPV13
]
), where the order in which quantum operations are applied can be subject to quantum uncertainty or may not be acyclic. This includes scenarios such as the quantum switch
[
CDPV13
]
, which involves a quantum superposition of Alice acting before Bob and Bob acting before Alice on a target quantum system (possibly depending on the state of a control system), as well as purely classical scenarios where there is a cyclic dependence between the operations of the parties (such as the Baumeler-Wolf process
[
BW16b
]
).
One such prominent framework is that of process matrices
[
OCB12
]
. Here one considers
N
parties associated with labs
A_{1},...,A_{N}
where just as in the BLO framework each lab is associated with a pair of in and output spaces
\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{in}}}
and
\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{out}}}
. The process matrix
\sigma\in\mathcal{L}(\bigotimes_{i}\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{in}}})\otimes\mathcal{L}(\bigotimes_{i}\mathcal{H}_{A_{i}^{\textup{out}}})
models the environment of these labs and tells us how they can be connected.
The process operator
\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}
of the BLO formalism, when expressed in the basis-dependent convention for CJ operators (without the duals) is precisely the process matrix
\sigma
. Given such a process operator or process matrix together with a set of local quantum channels
\mathcal{M}_{x_{i}|a_{i}}
, and the same probability rule
equation

122
can be used to compute the joint probability
\textup{Pr}_{\textup{BLO}}(x_{1},...,x_{N}|a_{1},...,a_{N})
. Recall that the form of this rule is independent of whether we use the basis-independent version of the BLO framework (with the dual spaces) or the standard basis-dependent version of the CJ isomorphism.

On the top left is an example of bipartite process matrix

In the BLO formalism, the process operator
\sigma^{A_{1},...,A_{N}}
is associated with a unitary channel on the parties outputs to their inputs, and this is linked to the process operator having further internal structure as a factorisation in terms of the channels
\sigma_{A_{i}|\mathrm{Pa}(A_{i})}
. While the BLO formalism includes certain classes of indefinite causal order process such as the quantum switch, it cannot model more general non-unitary processes (for instance the causal inequality violating process proposed by Oreshkov, Costa and Brukner
[
OCB12
]
).

In the earlier section, we discussed how to faithfully map tensor restricted BLO causal models to our framework. More generally, one
can also formulate all process matrices within our formalism through a generic mapping, which is similar to mappings proposed from process matrices to other cyclic quantum causality frameworks
[
LMGP+11a
,
LMGP+11b
]
and
[
VR24a
,
VR24b
]
(we will discuss such frameworks shortly). While this gives alternative and equivalent ways to study processes matrices (and in particular the resulting probabilities), it will generally not be a faithful mapping. The mapping is rather simple, it involves including
2N+1
vertices
\{A_{1}
,…,
A_{N}\}\cup\{X_{1}
,…,
X_{N}\}\cup\{\sigma\}
in the causal graph where all the
A_{i}
vertices and
\sigma
are unobserved and all
X_{i}
vertices are observed. The vertex
\sigma
associated with the channel whose CJ operator is the process matrix
\sigma
, while for the remaining vertices the channels associated with them are given by the chosen local operations in the lab through the same procedure as we used the previous section for BLO-QCM
⊗
s. The generic graph for all processes would be the one where we have a directed cycle
(\sigma,A_{i})
and
(A_{i},\sigma)
for each
A_{i}
, along with an edge
(A_{i},X_{i})
for every agent (see
figure

2
for an example).

The generic graph constructed above has a high connectivity, a process where neither
A
nor
B
causally influence the other would also be mapped to the same graph where the lack of causal influence between the parties cannot be discerned from the graphical representation alone. This implies that the model is unfaithful: the graph shows connectivity although we will observe independences in the joint probability distribution. There is scope to employ additional procedures to fine-grain the
\sigma
vertex of this graph into multiple vertices and thereby fine-grain the causal model (while preserving the overall behaviour of the channel
\sigma
) to discern more information on the causal structure. For instance such a notion of fine-graining for causal networks has been formally developed in
[
VR24a
,
VR24b
]
. Fine-graining has the potential to transform cyclic into acyclic causal models
[
VR24a
,
VR24b
]
as well as unfaithful into faithful causal models
[
GV24
]
while preserving the overall action of the channels involved. We leave an exploration of fine-graining in the context of causal inference in cyclic quantum causal models for future work.

Appendix C
Functional causal models and connection with
[
FGV25
]

In a related work
[
FGV25
]
, we define the probability rule for arbitrary cyclic functional causal models.
There, we use the same ideas of mapping a functional models on a cyclic graph to a functional causal model on an acyclic graph with post-selection, making use of a classical analogue of post-selected teleportation.
For further details on the classical framework see
[
FGV25
]
.
In this section, we show that classical functional models can be embedded in our quantum causal modelling framework and prove that the probability rule given in definition 12 of
[
FGV25
]
is equivalent to
definition

12
applied to the embedded casual model.
First, we briefly review functional causal models. Then, we define a mapping from functional causal models to causal models (
definition

2
). Finally, we prove consistency between the results of
[
FGV25
]
and the quantum formalism presented here.

C.1
Review of functional models

Classical causal models
[
Pea09
]
, also known as functional or structural causal models, describe how variables are related to each other through deterministic functions and are used for classical causal inference between classical random variables.
The general definition of functional causal models allows for continuous variables. However, in what follows we restrict the discussion to finite random variables.
Therefore, all functional causal models considered in this section belong to the subset fCM
{}_{\textup{finite}}
(see
figure

1
). For brevity, we denote a finite functional causal model on a graph
G
as
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
.

Definition 32

(Finite functional causal model)
.

Given a directed graph
G=(V,E)
, a finite functional model
(
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
)
is given by associating the following specifications to each vertex
v\in V
:

1.

A random variable
X_{v}
taking values
x_{v}

from a non-empty finite set
\mathcal{X}_{v}
. We will use a notation where if
V^{\prime}\subseteq V
is a non-empty subset of vertices,

\mathcal{X}_{V^{\prime}}=\prod_{v\in V^{\prime}}\mathcal{X}_{v}

(131)

where
\prod
here denotes the Cartesian product.

2.

An error random variable
U_{v}
taking values
u_{v}

from a finite set
\mathcal{U}_{v}
, distributed as
p^{v}:\mathcal{U}_{v}\mapsto[0,1]
.

3.

A function

f^{v}:\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)}\times\mathcal{U}_{v}\mapsto\mathcal{X}_{v}
.

In literature, the probability is considered to be well-defined for all functional models on
acyclic
graphs
[
Pea09
]
and for a restricted set of
cyclic
functional models
[
FM17
,
BFPM21
]
.
In definition 12 of
[
FGV25
]
, we provided a probability rule over the vertices of any — except for a handful of pathological cases — cyclic functional models. In the special case of acyclic models, the probability is defined as follows in the literature (and recovered by the general rule of
[
FGV25
]
).

Definition 33

(Probability distribution of an acyclic functional model)
.

Consider
a functional model
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
on an
acyclic
graph
G=(V,E)
and a global observed event
x:=\{x_{v}\in\mathcal{X}_{v}\}_{v\in V}
. The probability
\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}\left(x\right)_{G}\in[0,1]
is defined as

\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}\left(x\right)_{G}=\sum_{u}\prod_{v\in V}p^{v}(u_{v})\delta_{x_{v},f^{v}\left(x_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)},u_{v}\right)},

(132)

where the sum
\sum_{u}
runs over
u=\{u_{v}\in\mathcal{U}_{v}\}_{v\in V}
.

If a subset of vertices is unobserved, the distribution over the remaining observed vertices is obtained through marginalising
definition

33
over the unobserved variables.

C.2
Mapping a functional model to a causal model

Classical systems are naturally embedded into quantum mechanical systems. Indeed, they correspond to systems whose state belongs to a subset of density operators, namely states which are diagonal in a given fixed basis, the so-called
computational
basis.
Classical causal modelling, involving classical states and functional causal mechanisms is also naturally embedded into quantum causal modelling.
In this section, we define a map from functional causal models to causal models which preserves the acyclic probability
definition

33
through
definition

3
.

Causal graph.

Functional models are defined over graphs, not causal graphs. Hence, we first need to define causal graphs associated to functional models. Since these involve classical random variables, all edges of the causal graph are classical. Without loss of generality, we consider all vertices to be observed. If some vertices are unobserved, the probability distribution over the remaining ones is obtained though marginalising the joint distribution over the unobserved variables. Hence, it is not restrictive to consider all vertices as observed and eventually marginalise over unobserved ones.

Definition 34

(Causal graph of a functional model)
.

Given a functional model on a directed graph
G=(V,E)
, we define a causal graph by decorating
G
such that all vertices are observed,
V=V_{\textup{o}}
, and all edges are classical,
E=E_{\textup{cl}}
. Hence, all edges of the graph are represented as

, and all vertices are represented as

v

.

Notice that the outgoing edges of an observed vertex are necessarily classical, since all edges are classical, which proves that
definition

34
gives a well-defined causal graph.

Causal model.

Mapping a functional causal model to a causal model as in
definition

2
, involves describing classical objects, such as random variables and functional dependencies, as quantum ones.
Recall that, given a finite set
\mathcal{X}
, we associate to it a finite dimensional Hilbert space, such that
\dim(\mathcal{H}\hskip-1.0pt\left(\mathcal{X}\right))=|\mathcal{X}|
and label the elements of an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{H}\hskip-1.0pt\left(\mathcal{X}\right)
as
|x\rangle
for
x\in\mathcal{X}
, i.e.,

\mathcal{H}\hskip-1.0pt\left(\mathcal{X}\right)=\text{{span}}\left\{\;|x\rangle\;|\;x\in\mathcal{X}\right\}.

This allows us to describe classical random variables.
In addition, functional dependencies can be described using quantum channels as follows.

Definition 35
.

Let us consider a function
f:\mathcal{Y}\mapsto\mathcal{X}
, where
\mathcal{X}
and
\mathcal{Y}
are finite sets.
We define a POVM
E^{f}=\{E_{x}^{f}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\subseteq\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{H}\hskip-1.0pt\left(\mathcal{Y}\right)\right)
, as

E_{x}^{f}=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\delta_{x,f(y)}|y\rangle\langle y|.

(133)

For all functions
f:\mathcal{Y}\mapsto\mathcal{X}
, we have

\mathrm{Tr}\left[E_{x}^{f}|y\rangle\langle y|\right]=\delta_{x,f(y)}.

(134)

In addition,
\{E_{x}^{f}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}}
is a POVM, since
E_{x}^{f}
are positive and it holds

\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}E^{x}_{f}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathcal{X}\\
y\in\mathcal{Y}\end{subarray}}\delta_{x,f(y)}|y\rangle\langle y|=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in\mathcal{Y}\\
\exists x\in\mathcal{X}:f(y)=x\end{subarray}}|y\rangle\langle y|=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}|y\rangle\langle y|=\mathbbm{1}.

(135)

With these results in mind, we proceed to describe functional models within our causal modelling framework.

Definition 36

(Causal model associated to a functional model)
.

Consider a functional model
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
(
definition

32
) on a directed graph
G=(V,E)
. Using the same notation of
definition

32
, we define a causal model
\mathsf{Cm}(\mathsf{fCm})_{G}
on the causal graph given by
definition

34
, through:

1.

To each edge
e\in E=(v,v^{\prime})
associate the finite dimensional Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}_{e}=\mathcal{H}\hskip-1.0pt\left(\mathcal{X}_{v}\right)
, where
\mathcal{H}\hskip-1.0pt\left(\mathcal{X}_{v}\right)
is defined as in
equation

1
;

2.

To each error variable
U_{v}
of
v\in V
associate the finite dimensional Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}\hskip-1.0pt\left(\mathcal{U}_{v}\right)
, where
\mathcal{H}\hskip-1.0pt\left(\mathcal{U}_{v}\right)
is defined as in
equation

1
, and the state

\sigma^{v}=\sum_{u_{v}\in\mathcal{U}_{v}}p^{v}(u_{v})|u_{v}\rangle\langle u_{v}|_{\mathcal{H}\hskip-1.0pt\left(\mathcal{U}_{v}\right)};

(136)

3.

To each vertex
v\in V
associate the finite set
\mathcal{X}_{v}
as outcome set;

4.

To each vertex
v\in V
associate the set of CP maps

\left\{\mathcal{M}_{x}^{v}:\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{In}(v)}\right)\mapsto\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{Out}(v)}\right)\right\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{v}}

(137)

defined as follows: for all
\rho\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{In}(v)})
,

\mathcal{M}_{x}^{v}(\rho)=\mathrm{Tr}\left[E_{x}^{f^{v}}(\rho\otimes\sigma^{v})\right]\bigotimes_{e\in\mathrm{Out}(v)}|x\rangle\langle x|_{\mathcal{H}_{e}},

(138)

where
\{E_{x}^{f^{v}}\}_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{v}}
is the POVM obtained through applying
definition

35
to the function
f^{v}:\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)}\times\mathcal{U}_{v}\mapsto\mathcal{X}_{v}
and
\sigma^{v}
is defined in
equation

136
.

The following lemma proves that given an acyclic functional causal model
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
, the probability distribution evaluated using
definition

33
equals the probability distribution of the image causal model (
definition

36
),
\mathsf{Cm}(\mathsf{fCm})_{G}
evaluated using
definition

3
.

Lemma 37

(Equivalence of ayclic probabilities under
definition

36
)
.

Consider a functional model on a directed and acyclic graph
G=(V,E)
,
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
, and its image under the mapping of
definition

36
,
\mathsf{Cm}(\mathsf{fCm})_{G}
.
Let
x:=\{x_{v}\in\mathcal{X}_{v}\}_{v\in V}
be a joint observed event, then we have:

\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}(x)_{G}=\hyperlink{probacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{acyc}}}}(x)_{G},

(139)

where
\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}_{G}
is the acyclic probability distribution of
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
, evaluated with
definition

33
, and
\hyperlink{probacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{acyc}}}}_{G}
the acyclic probability distribution of
\mathsf{Cm}(\mathsf{fCm})_{G}
, evaluated using
definition

3
.

Proof.

For all
v\in V
, let us consider the action of
\mathcal{M}_{x_{v}}^{v}
on states of the form

|x_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)}\rangle\langle x_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)}|:=\bigotimes_{v^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Pa}(v)}|x_{v^{\prime}}\rangle\langle x_{v^{\prime}}|,

(140)

where
x_{v^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{X}_{v^{\prime}}
for all
v^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Pa}(v)
. Using
equation

134
and linearity of the trace, we have

\mathcal{M}_{x_{v}}^{v}\left(|x_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)}\rangle\langle x_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)}|\right)=\sum_{u_{v}\in\mathcal{U}_{v}}p^{v}(u_{v})\delta_{x_{v},f^{v}(x_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)},u_{v})}\bigotimes_{e\in\mathrm{Out}(v)}|x_{v}\rangle\langle x_{v}|_{\mathcal{H}_{e}}.

(141)

The maps associated to vertices are composed according to the graph connectivity (see
definition

3
for more details) taking as input
1\in\mathbb{C}
. In addition, the output of any CP map
\mathcal{M}_{x}^{v}
is always decohered in the basis specified by the values of
x_{v}
(this is always the case for maps associated to observed vertices). Thus, the input of all maps is always of the form considered in
equation

141
, up to a constant factor.
Since the graph is finite and acyclic, the output of the maps composition will eventually be in
\mathbb{C}
.
By linearity and because of trace-preservation, such composition will equal the product of the proportionality factors mentioned above, i.e.,
\sum_{u_{v}}p^{v}(u_{v})\delta_{x_{v},f^{v}(x_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)},u_{v})}
for each
v\in V
.

Thus, applying
definition

3
gives

\begin{split}\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}(x)_{G}=\bigcomp_{v\in V}\mathcal{M}_{x_{v}}^{v}=&\prod_{v\in V}\sum_{u_{v}\in\mathcal{U}_{v}}p^{v}(u_{v})\delta_{x_{v},f^{v}(x_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)},u_{v})}\\
=&\sum_{u_{V}}\prod_{v\in V}p^{v}(u_{v})\delta_{x_{v},f^{v}\left(x_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)},u_{v}\right)}=\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}\left(x\right)_{G},\end{split}

(142)

where the sum
\sum_{u_{V}}
runs over
u_{V}=\{u_{v}\in\mathcal{U}_{v}\}_{v\in V}
and
x=\{x_{v}\}_{v\in V}
.
Thus proving the equivalence of this definition and
definition

33
.
∎

Remark.

We described functional models within our framework as causal models on a causal graph having only observed vertices. In the functional modelling literature, if a vertex is unobserved the probability distribution over the remaining ones is obtained through marginalising the joint distribution. Within our framework, unobserved variables can be naturally represented as unobserved vertices of the causal graph. Consider a functional model as in
definition

32
, and assume that a subset of vertices are unobserved,
V_{\textup{u}}\subseteq V
. Then, we associate to this graph a causal graph where all edges are classical,
E=E_{\textup{cl}}
, the unobserved vertices are
V_{\textup{u}}
and the observed are
V_{\textup{o}}=V\setminus V_{\textup{u}}
. We define a causal model on this causal graph by preserving the same associations of
definition

36
to edges, observed vertices
v\in V_{\textup{o}}
and all error variables.
However, to each unobserved vertex
v\in V_{\textup{u}}
, we associate the CPTP map such that, for all
\rho\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{In}(v)})
,

\mathcal{E}^{v}(\rho)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{v}}\mathcal{M}_{x}^{v}(\rho)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{v}}\mathrm{Tr}\left[E_{x}^{f^{v}}(\rho\otimes\sigma^{v})\right]\bigotimes_{e\in\mathrm{Out}(v)}|x\rangle\langle x|_{\mathcal{H}_{e}},

(143)

where
\rho_{x}^{v}
and
\mathcal{M}_{x}^{v}
are as in
definition

36
.

The probability distribution of this causal model, evaluated through
definition

3
, gives for all
x=\{x_{v}\in\mathcal{X}_{v}\}_{v\in V}

\begin{split}\hyperlink{probacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{acyc}}}}\left(\{x_{v}\}_{v\in V_{\textup{o}}}\right)_{G}&=\bigcomp_{v\in V_{\textup{o}}}\mathcal{M}_{x_{v}}^{v}\bigcomp_{v^{\prime}\in V_{\textup{u}}}\mathcal{E}^{v^{\prime}}=\sum_{\{x_{v}\}_{v\in V_{\textup{u}}}}\bigcomp_{v\in V}\mathcal{M}_{x_{v}}^{v}\\
&=\sum_{\{x_{v}\}_{v\in V_{\textup{u}}}}\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}\left(x\right)_{G}=\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}\left(\{x_{v}\}_{v\in V_{\textup{o}}}\right)_{G}.\end{split}

(144)

where the sum runs over
\{x_{v}\in\mathcal{X}_{v}\}_{v\in V_{\textup{u}}}
.
Therefore, the distribution of the causal model which accounts for unobserved vertices in the causal graph is equal to the distribution obtained through marginalising
definition

33
over variables associated to unobserved vertices.

C.3
Equivalence of
p
-separation definitions

In a companion paper
[
FGV25
]
, we provide a causal modelling framework for cyclic classical causal models. This follows the same ideas of this work in mapping a given cyclic functional model to a family of acyclic models with post-selections. However, the mapping in section 3 of
[
FGV25
]
is constructed on a slightly different family of acyclic graphs which simplifies the mapping in the classical case without relying on the quantum notation and formalism used in this paper
20
20

20

The simplification is possible as classical variables can be copied and broadcast to multiple parties, i.e., the children vertices of the variable.
.
The graph family of
definition

6
plays a crucial role in defining
p
-separation (
definition

21
), while in
[
FGV25
]
,
p
-separation defined with respect to this slightly modified family. Here, we show that the two definitions of
p
-separation, which only depend on the graph, are equivalent.
Let us first comment on the two different graph families.

One graph, two acyclic families.

Given a (causal) graph
G
, we constructed a family of acyclic causal graph as in
definition

6
. This is denoted as
\mathbb{G}_{\textsc{tp}}(G)
, and defined above. For completeness, let us repeat the definition of
\mathbb{G}_{\textsc{tp}}(G)
.
See
[use
cref
not
ref
]

From the same underlying graph
G
, in definition 7 of
[
FGV25
]
we introduce a different family of acyclic graphs. We provide the definition of this family, which is denoted as
\mathbb{G}_{c,\textsc{tp}}{(G)}
, here.

Definition 38

(Family of acyclic classical teleportation graphs
\mathbb{G}_{c,\textsc{tp}}{(G)}
)
.

Given a directed graph
G=(V,E)
,
we define an associated family
\mathbb{G}_{c,\textsc{tp}}{(G)}
of acyclic graphs, where each element
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}\in\mathbb{G}_{c,\textsc{tp}}{(G)}
is obtained from the graph
G
as follows.

1.

Choose any subset of vertices
V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})\subseteq V
, such that the subgraph
G^{\prime}=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime})
of
G
with
V^{\prime}=V
and
E^{\prime}=E\setminus\left(\bigcup_{v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})}\mathrm{Out}(v)\right)
is acyclic. We refer to
V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})
as the split vertices of
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
.

2.

The vertices
V_{c,\textsc{tp}}
of
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
consist of the vertices
V
of the original graph
G
together with new vertices
R_{v},T_{v}
for each split vertex
v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})
, i.e.,

\displaystyle V_{c,\textsc{tp}}=V\cup\{R_{v}\}_{v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})}\cup\{T_{v}\}_{v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})}.

(145)

3.

The edges
E_{c,\textsc{tp}}
of
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
consist of the edges
E^{\prime}
of the subgraph
G^{\prime}
together with the following new edges:

\displaystyle E_{c,\textsc{tp}}=E^{\prime}\cup\{(v,T_{v})\}_{v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})}

\displaystyle\cup\{(R_{v},T_{v})\}_{v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})}

\displaystyle\cup\{(R_{v},v^{\prime})\}_{v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}}),v^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Ch}(v)_{G}},

(146)

where
\mathrm{Ch}(v)_{G}
refers to the children vertices of
v
in the graph
G
.

For each
v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})
, we refer to the vertices
R_{v}
and
T_{v}
as pre- and post-selection vertices respectively and depict them with distinct vertex styles

T_{v}

and

R_{v}

, as these will play a special role in our framework.
This construction makes
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
identical to
G
up to replacing all vertices
v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})
with the following structure

(147)

Each element of the family
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}\in\mathbb{G}_{c,\textsc{tp}}{(G)}
is called a classical
teleportation graph
. The set of all pre- and post-selection vertices in
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
are denoted as
V_{\textup{pre}}=\{R_{v}\}_{v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})}
and
V_{\textup{post}}=\{T_{v}\}_{v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})}
.

Definition

6
is formulated in terms of causal graphs while
definition

38
is not. However, we can equivalently consider a causal graph where all vertices are observed in
definition

38
(consistently with the notation used in
equation

147
)and compare the two definitions.

With this in mind, the family of acyclic graphs of
definition

38
is constructed in a similar way to the family of acyclic teleportation graphs in
definition

6
.
Specifically, both definitions involve considering an acyclic subgraph of
G
. The subgraphs that are used to construct
definition

38
are a subset of those considered for
definition

6
. Indeed, in the latter, one can remove any subset of edges from
G
to make graph acyclic, while in
definition

38
one removes all outgoing edges from a subset of vertices
V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})
.
In addition, in the classical case all outgoing edges are jointly substituted with one pair of pre- and post-selection vertices, while, in the teleportation graph family of
definition

6
, each split edge is associated to a pair of pre- and post-selection vertices.

To understand the difference between these two families, consider the cyclic graph,
G_{\textup{eg}}
, and its subgraphs,
G_{\textup{eg}}^{\prime}
and
G_{\textup{eg}}^{\prime\prime}
.

(148)

The acyclic sugraph
G_{\textup{eg}}^{\prime}
is a valid acyclic subraph for both
definitions

6
and
38
, respectively with set of split edges
E_{\textsc{s}}(G_{\textup{eg}}^{\prime})=\{(A,B),(A,C)\}
and split vertices
V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{\textup{eg}})=\{A\}
. While, the acyclic subgraph
G_{\textup{eg}}^{\prime\prime}
, which has set of split edges
E_{\textsc{s}}(G_{\textup{eg}}^{\prime\prime})=\{(A,B),(C,A)\}
, is not valid for
definition

38
.

definitions

6
and
38
constructed from
G_{\textup{eg}}^{\prime}
, are, respectively,

(152)

The left hand side represents the structure of
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}
and the right hand side,
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
, and where the red vertices correspond to the post-selection vertices in both cases.
Then it is easy to see that
(V_{1}\perp^{d}V_{2}|V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}})_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}}
implies
(V_{1}\perp^{d}V_{2}|V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime})_{{G_{\textsc{tp}}}}
, where
V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime}
is the set of all post-selection vertices in
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}
. By
definition

21
of
p
-separation,
(V_{1}\perp^{d}V_{2}|V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime})_{{G_{\textsc{tp}}}}
implies
(V_{1}\perp^{p}V_{2}|V_{3})_{G}
as required.

(
\perp^{p}\implies\perp^{p,c}
)
: If
(V_{1}\perp^{p}V_{2}|V_{3})_{G}
, then there exists
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}\in\mathbb{G}_{\textsc{tp}}(G)
such that
(V_{1}\perp^{d}V_{2}|V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}})_{{G_{\textsc{tp}}}}
where
V_{\textup{post}}
denotes the set of all post-selection vertices in
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}
(
definition

21
). Let
E_{\textsc{s}}({G_{\textsc{tp}}})
be the set of split edges of
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}
and define

V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}}):=\{v\in V\text{ s.t. }\exists e=(v,v^{\prime})\in E_{\textsc{s}}({G_{\textsc{tp}}})\}.

(153)

Consider the graph
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}\in\mathbb{G}_{\textsc{tp}}(G)
such that
E_{\textsc{s}}(G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}})=\bigcup_{v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})}\mathrm{Out}(v)
. We want to prove that
(V_{1}\perp^{d}V_{2}|V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime})_{G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}}
, where
V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime}
denotes the set of post-selection vertices in
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
.

Let us consider
v_{1}\in V_{1}
and
v_{2}\in V_{2}
, if these are
d
-separated conditioned on
v_{3},V_{\textup{post}}
in
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}
, then one of the following conditions is satisfied:

•

There is no path (even undirected) between
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
in
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}
.
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
can be obtained through substituting some edges of
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}
with a pre- and post-selection edges and vertices. Such substitution does not create new paths, hence there is also no path between
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
in
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
.

•

All paths between
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
are blocked by
V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}
. Hence, for each path in
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}
, one of the following holds:

\circ

There exists
W\in V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}
such that
A\leftarrow W\rightarrow B
for some
A
and
B
in the path. Adding pre and post-selection edges and vertices does not change the path, hence, the difference between
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}
and
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
is that some edges of the path might be substituted with such vertices and edges. If this substitution does not involve the subgraph
A\leftarrow W\rightarrow B
, then the same
W
blocks the path in
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
. If the edge
A\leftarrow W
is substituted, we have
A\leftarrow Q\rightarrow P\leftarrow W\rightarrow B
. Since, the path between
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
contains
P\leftarrow W\rightarrow B
and
W\in V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime}
, then the path is blocked in
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
. The same considerations hold if the edge
W\rightarrow B
is substituted.

\circ

There exists
W\in V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}
such that
A\rightarrow W\rightarrow B
for some
A
and
B
in the path. Adding pre and post-selection edges and vertices does not change the path, hence, the difference between
{G_{\textsc{tp}}}
and
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
is that some edges of the path might be substituted with a teleportation subgraph. If this substitution does not involve the subgraph
A\rightarrow W\rightarrow B
, then the same vertex
W
blocks the path also in
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
. If the edge
A\rightarrow W
is substituted, we have
A\rightarrow P\leftarrow Q\rightarrow W\rightarrow B
. Since the path between
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
contains
Q\rightarrow W\rightarrow B
and
W\in V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime}
, then the path is blocked in
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
. The same considerations hold if the edge
W\rightarrow B
is substituted.

\circ

There exists
U
such that
A\rightarrow U\leftarrow B
for some
A
and
B
in the path and
U
nor any descendent of
U
are in
V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}
. Assume first that the substitution of edges with pre and post-selection vertices and edges does not involve the subgraph
A\rightarrow U\leftarrow B
, but that there is a descendent of
U
in the conditioning set, i.e.,
W\in V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime}
such that

(155)

Hence,
W^{\prime}\in V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}
and it is a descendent of
U
. This is not possible by hypothesis, meaning that even in
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
,
U
has no descendents in the conditioning set. If the edge
A\rightarrow U
is substituted, we have
A\rightarrow P\leftarrow Q\rightarrow U\leftarrow B
. The path between
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
contains
Q\rightarrow U\leftarrow B
, hence the path is blocked in
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
. The same considerations hold if the edge
U\leftarrow B
is substituted.

This proves that if
(V_{1}\perp^{d}V_{2}|V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}})_{{G_{\textsc{tp}}}}
, then
(V_{1}\perp^{d}V_{2}|V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime})_{G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}}
. Using
equation

152
to relate
G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}
and
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
, it holds that
(V_{1}\perp^{d}V_{2}|V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime})_{G^{\prime}_{\textsc{tp}}}
implies
(V_{1}\perp^{d}V_{2}|V_{3}\cup V_{\textup{post}}^{\textup{c}})_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}}
.
∎

Thus,
p
-separation relations of a given graph
G
can be equivalently deduced using
definition

21
or
definition

39
.

C.4
Equivalence of cyclic probabilities under the mapping in
definition

36

In
section

C.2
, we showed that applying
definition

36
to map an acyclic functional model to an acyclic causal model preserves the probability distribution over observed events.
In this section, we consider probabilities over cyclic functional models and show that the probability rule given in definition 12 of
[
FGV25
]
is equivalent to applying the probability rule of
definition

12
to the image causal models through
definition

36
.

Lemma 41
.

Consider a functional model on a directed graph
G=(V,E)
,
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
, and its image under the mapping of
definition

36
,
\mathsf{Cm}(\mathsf{fCm})_{G}
. Let
x=\{x_{v}\in\mathcal{X}_{v}\}_{v\in V}
be a joint observed event, then we have:

\hyperlink{probf}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}_{\mathrm{f}}}(x)_{G}=\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}(x)_{G}

(156)

where
\hyperlink{probf}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}_{\mathrm{f}}}_{G}
is the probability distribution of
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
evaluated with definition 12 of
[
FGV25
]
and
\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}_{G}
is the probability distribution given by
definition

12
of
\mathsf{Cm}(\mathsf{fCm})_{G}
.

Proof.

In the proof the following two results are used.

Lemma 42
.

Consider a functional model on a directed graph
G=(V,E)
with functional dependencies
f^{v}:\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{Pa}(v)}\times\mathcal{U}_{v}\mapsto\mathcal{X}_{v}
, associated to each vertex
v\in V
. The maps
\mathcal{M}_{x}^{f^{v}}
obtained though
definition

36
, satisfy

\mathcal{D}_{E_{\textup{out}}}\circ\mathcal{M}_{x}^{f^{v}}\circ\mathcal{D}_{E_{\textup{in}}}=\mathcal{M}_{x}^{f^{v}}

(157)

for any subset of outgoing and ingoing edges to
v
,
E_{\textup{out}}\subseteq\mathrm{Out}(v)
and
E_{\textup{in}}\subseteq\mathrm{In}(v)
. The decohering channel
\mathcal{D}_{E^{\prime}}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{E^{\prime}})\mapsto\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{E^{\prime}})
is defined for any subset of edges
E^{\prime}\subseteq E
as
\mathcal{D}_{E^{\prime}}=\bigotimes_{e\in E}\mathcal{D}_{e}
acting as
\mathcal{D}_{e}(\rho)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{e}}|x\rangle\langle x|\rho|x\rangle\langle x|
for any
\rho\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{e})
.

Proof.

Let us prove that

\mathcal{D}_{e}\circ\mathcal{M}_{x}^{f^{v}}=\mathcal{M}_{x}^{f^{v}}=\mathcal{M}_{x}^{f^{v}}\circ\mathcal{D}_{e^{\prime}}

(158)

for any
e\in\mathrm{Out}(v)
and
e^{\prime}\in\mathrm{In}(v)
. Once this is proven the general results follows from iterative application of this equality.
The first equality follows immediately from the form of
\mathcal{M}_{x}^{v}
, since for all
\rho\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{In}(v)})
, we have

\mathcal{M}_{x}^{v}(\rho)=\mathrm{Tr}\left[E_{x}^{f^{v}}(\rho\otimes\sigma^{v})\right]\bigotimes_{e\in\mathrm{Out}(v)}|x\rangle\langle x|_{\mathcal{H}_{e}},

(159)

which is already coherence-free.
The second follows from the form of
E_{x}^{f^{v}}
and of the state
\sigma^{v}
(see
equation

136
), indeed

\begin{split}\mathrm{Tr}\left(E_{x}^{f^{v}}(\mathcal{D}_{e^{\prime}}(\rho)\otimes\sigma^{v})\right)&=\mathrm{Tr}\left(E_{x}^{f^{v}}\mathcal{D}_{e^{\prime}\cup U_{v}}(\rho\otimes\sigma^{v})\right)\\
&=\mathrm{Tr}\left(\sum_{y}\delta_{x,f^{v}(y)}|y\rangle\langle y|\mathcal{D}_{\tilde{e}}(\tilde{\rho})\right)\\
&=\sum_{y}\sum_{z}\delta_{x,f^{v}(y)}\mathrm{Tr}\left(|y\rangle\langle y||z\rangle\langle z|\tilde{\rho}|z\rangle\langle z|\right)\\
&=\sum_{y}\delta_{x,f^{v}(y)}\mathrm{Tr}\left(|y\rangle\langle y|(\rho\otimes\sigma^{v})\right)=\mathrm{Tr}\left(E_{x}^{f^{v}}(\rho\otimes\sigma^{v})\right).\end{split}

(160)

where we denoted
\tilde{e}=e^{\prime}\cup U_{v}
and
\tilde{\rho}=\rho\otimes\sigma^{v}
for brevity, and the sums run over
y=\{y_{v^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{X}_{v^{\prime}}\}_{v^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Pa}(v)}\cup\{u_{v}\in\mathcal{U}_{v}\}
and
z=\{z_{v^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{X}_{v^{\prime}}\}_{v^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Pa}(v)}\cup\{u^{\prime}_{v}\in\mathcal{U}_{v}\}
.
∎

Lemma 43
.

Consider a Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{In}(v)}=\bigotimes_{e\in\mathrm{In}(v)}\mathcal{H}_{e}
22
22

22

The lemma holds for any Hilbert space with such partition. We call the space
\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{In}(v)}
since the lemma will be applied to subsystems in a causal model.
. For any
E_{x},\rho\in\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{In}(v)}\right)
and
E_{\textup{in}}\subseteq\mathrm{In}(v)
, it holds

\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\left[E_{x}(\mathcal{D}_{E_{\textup{in}}}(\rho))\right]=\mathrm{Tr}\left[(\mathcal{D}_{E_{\textup{in}}}(E_{x}))\rho\right].

(161)

Proof.

The proof follows from the cyclicity of the trace

\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\left[E_{x}(\mathcal{D}_{E_{\textup{in}}}(\rho)\right]=\sum_{y}\mathrm{Tr}\left[E_{x}(|y\rangle\langle y|_{E_{\textup{in}}}\otimes\mathbbm{1})\rho(|y\rangle\langle y|_{E_{\textup{in}}}\otimes\mathbbm{1})\right]

(162)

\displaystyle=\sum_{y}\mathrm{Tr}\left[(|y\rangle\langle y|_{E_{\textup{in}}}\otimes\mathbbm{1})E_{x}(|y\rangle\langle y|_{E_{\textup{in}}}\otimes\mathbbm{1})\rho\right]=\mathrm{Tr}\left[(\mathcal{D}_{E_{\textup{in}}}(E_{x}))\rho\right].

(163)

∎

Given these two results, we can proceed with the proof.

Overview of the proof and relevant notation.

The goal of this proof is to connect the probabilities of a functional causal model on a possibly cyclic graph
G
, namely
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
, and those of its image causal model through the embedding
definition

36
, namely
\mathsf{Cm}(\mathsf{fCm}_{G})
(which, for brevity, we will simply denote as
\mathsf{Cm}_{G}
in what follows). To achieve this, we define auxiliary functional models (
definition

32
) and causal models (
definition

2
). Although the idea behind the proof is straightforward, given our formalism, it involves relating a number of different causal graphs and causal models. We therefore first sketch the main steps and notation of the proof, before detailing it.

Step 0:

We start considering a functional causal model on
G
:
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
(
definition

32
).

The cyclic probability distribution for the observed event
x
relative to this functional model is
\hyperlink{probf}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}_{\mathrm{f}}}(x)_{G}
(definition 12 in
[
FGV25
]
).

Step 1:

We define a classical teleportation causal model on a teleportation graph
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
induced by
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
:
\mathsf{fCm}_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}}
(definition 9 of
[
FGV25
]
).

Let
V_{\textup{post}}
be the set of post-selection vertices in
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
, which is acyclic by construction, and
V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})
the set of split vertices of
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
.
The probability distribution of the event
x
and successful post-selections
\{t_{v}=1\}_{T_{v}\in V_{\textup{post}}}
relative to this acyclic
functional model is
\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}(x,\{t_{v}=1\}_{T_{v}\in V_{\textup{post}}})_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}}
(
definition

33
).

By definition, the probability distribution of the cyclic model
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
equals the conditional distribution of the acyclic model
\mathsf{fCm}_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}}
, i.e.,

\hyperlink{probf}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}_{\mathrm{f}}}(x)_{G}=\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}(x|\{t_{v}=1\}_{T_{v}\in V_{\textup{post}}})_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}}

(164)

for all observed events
x:=\{x_{v}\in\mathcal{X}_{v}\}_{v\in V}
.

Step 2:

We define an intermediate functional model on a graph
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}^{\prime}
which is constructed from the classical teleportation graph
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
:
\mathsf{fCm}_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}^{\prime}}
. The idea is to use the correspondence between a single broadcasted classical teleportation protocol and multiple copies of regular classical teleportation, in going from
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
to
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}^{\prime}
(
equation

152
).

Let

G_{c,\textsc{tp}}^{\prime}
.
The acyclic probability distribution of the event
x
and successful post-selections
\{t^{e}_{v}=1\}_{T^{e}_{v}\in V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime}}
relative to this functional model is
\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}(x,\{t^{e}_{v}=1\}_{T^{e}_{v}\in V_{\textup{post}}})_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}^{\prime}}
(
definition

).

We prove that the conditional probabilities in
\mathsf{fCm}_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}}
(from
Step 1
) and
\mathsf{fCm}_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}^{\prime}}
are equal, i.e.,

\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}(x|\{t^{e}_{v}=1\}_{T^{e}_{v}\in V_{\textup{post}}^{\prime}})_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}^{\prime}}=\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}(x|\{t_{v}=1\}_{T_{v}\in V_{\textup{post}}})_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}}.

Then, we define a classical teleportation functional model on
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
through definition 9 of
[
FGV25
]
. In particular, this construction prescribes that the same finite sets, functions and probabilities of the original functional model are associated to vertices and edges that are preserved from
G
to
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
. To pre- and post-selection vertices we associate uniform prior classical teleportation protocols
23
23

23

Any other choice of classical post-selected teleportation protocol would yield the same probability as this canonical choice, as shown in
[
FGV25
]
paper.
, i.e., for all
v\in V_{\textsc{s}}(G_{c,\textsc{tp}})
we associate to the corresponding pre-selection vertex
R_{v}
the finite set
\mathcal{X}_{R_{v}}=\mathcal{X}_{v}
, a uniform distribution to its error variable
p^{R_{v}}(u)=|\mathcal{X}_{v}|^{-1}
for all
u\in\mathcal{X}_{v}
and a function
f^{R_{v}}(u)=u
. Notice that this amounts to having the variable associated to pre-selection vertices
R_{v}
distributed as
p^{R_{v}}
(for more details see the remark in section 2 of
[
FGV25
]
), thus in what follows we will refer to
R_{v}
and its distribution.
We associate to the corresponding post-selection vertex
T_{v}
the finite set
\mathcal{X}_{T_{v}}=\{0,1\}
and a (deterministic) delta function
f^{T_{v}}(x,y)=\delta_{x,y}
for all
x,y\in\mathcal{X}_{v}
.

By definition 12 of
[
FGV25
]
, given an observed event
x:=\{x_{v}\in\mathcal{X}_{v}\}_{v\in V}
, the probability of
\mathsf{fCm}_{G}
is defined as

\hyperlink{probf}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}_{\mathrm{f}}}(x)_{G}=\hyperlink{probfacyc}{\hyperlink{prob}{\mathrm{Pr}}{{}_{\mathrm{f,acyc}}}}\left(x|\{t_{T}=1\}_{T\in V_{\textup{post}}}\right)_{G_{c,\textsc{tp}}},

(173)

where
V_{\textup{post}}
denotes the set of post-selection vertices of
G_{c,\textsc{tp}}
.
